headline: Medium risk: pdf.js can process attacker-controlled PDFs, but awesome-prompts is non-runnable and network-isolated, limiting pairwise injection and leakage pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-prompts is a content-writing, non-runnable repo with no I/O surfaces, so it cannot directly ingest pdf.js output. pdf.js does process PDF files and can render attacker-controlled document content, but the bridge between them is at most manual copy/paste or file handoff, making prompt injection possible only through unusual operator workflow.
conditions: IF an operator manually copies text from pdf.js-rendered content into awesome-prompts prompts, injection becomes plausible.
IF a shared workspace is introduced outside the current profiles, the pathway widens.
mitigations: Keep the agents in separate workflows with no copy/paste bridge.
Review PDF-derived text before pasting into prompt-writing tasks.
Use a plain-text sanitizer on extracted PDF text.
requires-engineering: add provenance labels to extracted content.
requires-engineering: isolate the two agents in separate workspaces.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have network_egress set to none, so there is no documented outbound exfiltration path. pdf.js touches PDF documents and files, while awesome-prompts touches no data classes. The pair can still leak locally if PDFs are manually moved into the content-writing workflow, but the blast radius is limited and no default upload path is shown.
conditions: IF PDF contents are manually copied into awesome-prompts artifacts, local leakage occurs.
IF either profile is later given network egress, leakage severity increases.
mitigations: Do not paste PDF text into prompt libraries unless necessary.
Store PDFs and prompt assets in separate directories.
Redact sensitive fields before transfer.
requires-engineering: enforce DLP checks on copied text.
requires-engineering: add access controls between workspaces.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: No overlapping write-capable mutable surface is documented. awesome-prompts is non-runnable and has no filesystem or network write permissions shown, while pdf.js only documents PDF-file handling and browser-based tests. Without a shared writable target, there is no plausible capability conflict pathway in the profiles.
conditions: IF a shared writable directory or git working tree is added, conflict risk must be reassessed.
mitigations: Keep outputs in separate folders.
Avoid concurrent edits to the same repository.
Use read-only mounts for PDF inputs.
requires-engineering: add file locking if a shared workspace is introduced.

D_cascading_error.rationale: pdf.js can produce extracted or rendered document text, but awesome-prompts is a prompt-writing repository rather than an action-taking agent. There is no documented default path where one agent's output is treated as authoritative by the other, so cascading error is limited to manual reuse of text by an operator.
conditions: IF pdf.js output is manually copied into prompt content without review, errors can propagate.
IF a downstream agent is added that acts on the prompt text, the risk increases.
mitigations: Verify extracted text against the source PDF.
Mark generated text as untrusted until reviewed.
Separate extraction from prompt-authoring steps.
requires-engineering: add validation for quoted facts.
requires-engineering: add human approval before reuse.

E_compliance.rationale: No residency, certification, retention, or regulated data-class mismatch is documented. awesome-prompts touches no data classes, and pdf.js only touches PDF documents with no stated PHI, EU PII, or special compliance scope. The profiles do not establish a compliance conflict pathway.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is introduced into PDF processing, compliance must be reassessed.
mitigations: Avoid processing regulated PDFs without a policy review.
Classify PDFs before use.
Keep compliance-sensitive documents out of the pair.
requires-engineering: add retention and residency controls if regulated data is introduced.
